subject: physics
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: Which particles are found in the nucleus of an atom?
questions.explain: The nucleus contains protons and neutrons, while electrons orbit it in shells.

questions.q: What is the relative electric charge of a neutron?
questions.explain: Neutrons are electrically neutral, so they have a relative charge of 0.

questions.q: The atomic (proton) number of an element is equal to the number of what?
questions.explain: The atomic number equals the number of protons, which defines the element.

questions.q: Isotopes of the same element have:
options: The same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons
The same number of neutrons but different numbers of protons
Different numbers of both protons and electrons
The same mass number but different atomic numbers
questions.explain: Isotopes share the proton number but differ in neutron number, giving different mass numbers.

questions.q: An atom has 11 protons and 12 neutrons. What is its mass number?
questions.explain: Mass number = protons + neutrons = 11 + 12 = 23.

questions.q: Roughly how does the radius of a nucleus compare with the radius of the whole atom?
options: The nucleus is about 10,000 times smaller than the atom
The nucleus is about the same size as the atom
The nucleus is about 10 times smaller than the atom
The nucleus is larger than the atom
questions.explain: An atom is around 10^-10 m across while the nucleus is around 10^-14 m, so the nucleus is far smaller.

questions.q: An alpha particle is identical to which of the following?
options: A helium nucleus (2 protons and 2 neutrons)
questions.explain: An alpha particle consists of 2 protons and 2 neutrons, the same as a helium nucleus.

questions.q: What is a beta (β⁻) particle?
options: A high-speed electron emitted from the nucleus
questions.explain: Beta-minus decay releases a fast-moving electron when a neutron changes into a proton.

questions.q: What is the unit of radioactive activity?
questions.explain: Activity is measured in becquerels, where 1 Bq is one nuclear decay per second.

questions.q: Which material is sufficient to stop alpha radiation?
questions.explain: Alpha particles are the least penetrating and are absorbed by paper or a few centimetres of air.

questions.q: Which type of nuclear radiation is the most strongly ionising?
questions.explain: Alpha particles are the most ionising because of their large charge and mass, though they are the least penetrating.

questions.q: Which type of radiation is stopped by a few millimetres of aluminium?
questions.explain: Beta particles pass through paper but are absorbed by a few millimetres of aluminium.

questions.q: What is meant by the half-life of a radioactive isotope?
options: The time taken for the number of undecayed nuclei (or the activity) to halve
The time taken for all the nuclei to decay
The time taken for the mass of the sample to double
The number of nuclei that decay each second
questions.explain: Half-life is the average time for half of the undecayed nuclei in a sample to decay.

questions.q: A radioactive source has an activity of 800 Bq and a half-life of 2 hours. What will its activity be after 6 hours?
questions.explain: 6 hours is 3 half-lives, so activity falls to 800 → 400 → 200 → 100 Bq.

questions.q: A sample starts with 1600 undecayed nuclei. After 4 half-lives, how many undecayed nuclei remain?
questions.explain: Each half-life halves the number: 1600 → 800 → 400 → 200 → 100.

questions.q: A carbon-14 nucleus (6 protons, mass number 14) undergoes beta-minus decay. What is the atomic number of the new nucleus?
questions.explain: In beta-minus decay a neutron becomes a proton, so the atomic number increases by 1, from 6 to 7.

questions.q: Which of the following is the largest single source of natural background radiation for most people in the UK?
questions.explain: Radon gas released from rocks and soil is the biggest contributor to natural background radiation in the UK.

questions.q: What is the difference between irradiation and contamination?
options: Irradiation is being exposed to radiation from an external source; contamination is having radioactive material on or in the body
Irradiation makes an object radioactive; contamination does not
Contamination only happens with gamma rays; irradiation only with alpha
There is no difference between them
questions.explain: Irradiation exposes an object to radiation without transferring material, whereas contamination means radioactive atoms are on or inside the object.

questions.q: Why is an alpha source suitable for use inside a household smoke detector?
options: Its short range means it is stopped by smoke particles and cannot travel far into the room
It is the most penetrating radiation and reaches every corner of the room
It produces no ionisation at all
It has an extremely long half-life of a few seconds
questions.explain: Alpha radiation ionises air over a short range and is easily blocked by smoke, making it safe and effective in detectors.

questions.q: Which isotope is commonly used as the fuel in a nuclear fission reactor?
questions.explain: Uranium-235 is a fissile isotope that splits when it absorbs a neutron, releasing energy in reactors.

questions.q: Which statement best describes nuclear fusion?
options: Two light nuclei join to form a heavier nucleus, releasing energy
A heavy nucleus splits into two lighter nuclei, releasing energy
A nucleus emits an alpha particle
An electron is captured by a proton
questions.explain: Fusion joins small nuclei, such as hydrogen isotopes, into a larger nucleus and releases energy, as happens in stars.

questions.q: In a nuclear fission reaction, what is released that can go on to cause further fission and sustain a chain reaction?
questions.explain: Each fission event releases neutrons that can be absorbed by other nuclei, causing a self-sustaining chain reaction.
